sections.content: Two production Laravel apps needed object storage this year — a travel platform and a gold exchange MIS — and both shipped on **MinIO**, self-hosted and served through Nginx. This is the real setup: the stack, the ports, and the config that made presigned URLs work behind the proxy.
Two Projects, One Storage Problem

**Travel platform (Laravel + Filament v5):** tour packages, destinations, galleries, review photos, and CSV imports uploaded daily from an admin panel. Earlier in the project every file landed on the local `public` disk — `APP_URL/storage` links that break the moment the server runs out of disk.

**Gold exchange MIS (Laravel + Filament v5):** KYC identity documents (PAN, passport, national ID cards as images and PDFs) plus purchase compliance paperwork — regulated records. Local-disk storage with a symlinked `public` folder was not a defensible place for them.
Why MinIO Instead of AWS S3

items: **Data residency** — regulated records stay inside the country's borders; no decision about which foreign region holds them
**Cost** — no per-GB storage fees, no egress charges; storage on an existing server is effectively free
**Zero code churn** — both apps already shipped the Laravel `s3` filesystem driver with AWS-style env keys; swapping in MinIO only changed endpoint, keys, and bucket
**No vendor lock-in** — the S3 API is the contract; move to another S3-compatible store without touching application code

sections.content: Proving the Driver with play.min.io

Before standing up any MinIO server, I validated the whole S3 stack against **play.min.io** — MinIO's public demonstration endpoint — from a PayloadCMS admin in the same stack and from the Laravel driver. The Payload environment pointed `S3_ENDPOINT=https://play.min.io`, and the Laravel CORS config whitelisted that origin. If signing, path-style addressing, and uploads worked against a public endpoint, the remaining work was only where to point the server.
Migrating the Travel Platform to MinIO

The `public` disk was already carrying real uploads, so the migration shipped as an idempotent artisan command that walks the local disk, streams every file into the MinIO bucket, and optionally deletes the local copy:
php artisan storage:move-to-minio --delete-local

After that, every Filament upload defaults to MinIO without per-field work — one `configureUsing` hook in `AppServiceProvider` sets `disk('minio')` on all `FileUpload` components. Destinations store into `destinations/featured` and `destinations/gallery`, packages into `packages/OG-Image`, plus review images, category images, and admin CSV uploads.
Two Disks, Two Security Models (Gold Exchange MIS)

'minio_private' => [
    'driver' => 's3',
    'key' => env('MINIO_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
    'secret' => env('MINIO_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
    'region' => env('MINIO_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
    'bucket' => env('MINIO_PRIVATE_BUCKET'),
    'endpoint' => env('MINIO_ENDPOINT', 'http://127.0.0.1:9091'),
    'use_path_style_endpoint' => true, // IMPORTANT for MinIO
    'url' => null, // force temporary URLs
    'visibility' => 'private',
],

'minio_public' => [
    'driver' => 's3',
    ...
    'endpoint' => env('MINIO_ENDPOINT', 'https://s3.example.com:9000'),
    'url' => env('MINIO_ENDPOINT') . '/' . env('MINIO_PUBLIC_BUCKET'),
    'visibility' => 'public',
],

The private disk is the important one. Setting `url => null` forces Laravel's S3 adapter into **temporary (presigned) URL** mode — KYC documents and purchase compliance files are never publicly addressable; Filament receives a short-lived signed link per request. Every `FileUpload` on the KYC and purchase forms points there with `->disk('minio_private')->visibility('private')` under the `kyc` and `Purchase Additional Documents` directories.
Ports and the Nginx Layout

MinIO's native ports stayed in the default family — API on **9000**, Console on **9001** — but the server ran on an internal endpoint (`127.0.0.1:9091` in one config's local default) with Nginx in front terminating TLS. Each side of MinIO gets its own virtual host:

The Laravel CORS whitelist is the audit trail for exactly which hosts this arrangement serves — `https://storage.example.com` and `https://console-storage.example.com` are live entries, with the local `http://localhost:9000` / `http://localhost:9001` dev origins commented out once the proxy replaced direct ports.
What Broke — and How It Was Fixed

items: **Presigned URLs pointed at the wrong host** — with the default endpoint `127.0.0.1:9091`, every temporary URL MinIO signed embedded that local address, so links worked only on the server itself. The fix was telling the application the external endpoint (`https://s3.example.com:9000`, via the Nginx host) so both the SDK calls and the generated URLs carry the reachable hostname. This is why the config carries the comment *"MinIO endpoint (API port, usually 9000)"* right next to the non-default 9091.

**Path-style vs virtual-host-style addressing** — MinIO behind a custom domain cannot answer virtual-host-style `bucket.host` requests without a wildcard `MINIO_DOMAIN`. Setting `use_path_style_endpoint => true` on both disks was mandatory, and both configs annotate it with *"IMPORTANT for MinIO"*.

**CORS in the browser console** — the Console and API live on different subdomains, and the admin panel loads directly in the browser. `allowed_origins` had to explicitly list the storage, console, and play-min.io origins, or signed browser uploads were silently blocked.

sections.content: Which Applications Consume It

items: **Travel platform backend (Laravel)** — `minio` disk through the S3 driver; all Filament uploads default there
**Gold exchange MIS (Laravel)** — `minio_private` + `minio_public` disks; KYC and purchase forms, creditor and debtor document fields
**PayloadCMS admin** — the same bucket family via its S3 adapter, first proven against `play.min.io`

sections.content: Why This Matters

Self-hosted object storage is not about avoiding AWS. It is about keeping regulated documents in-country, making storage cost a rounding error instead of a billed line, and preserving the S3 contract so nothing in the application cares what is behind it. The price is operational: a server to maintain, a proxy to keep sharp, and an endpoint convention you must never let drift — because every presigned URL inherits it. What I would change next: enforce bucket lifecycle rules and versioning, and stop shipping the Console on a public subdomain — the web UI should sit behind an allow-listed IP or a VPN.
